\chapter{He, She, and Whose}
\label{ch:te-he-she-and-whose}
\hlchaptermodality{79}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can talk about a third person in Telugu, mark a noun as an owner or an object, and address somebody respectfully.}

Complete TE-C79-garu and demonstrate the chapter promise.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[snēhituḍi]{\te{స్నేహితుడి} (snēhituḍi) — the friend's}

\label{lesson:TE-C79-friends}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{unnārā} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{స్నేహితుడి}}
\textbf{\te{స్నేహితుడి}} (\emph{snēhituḍi}) — \textquotedblleft{}the friend's\textquotedblright{}.

\te{నా} and \te{నీ} let you own things as \emph{I} and \emph{you}. Nothing let a named person own anything.

A Telugu noun becomes an owner by changing its own ending: \te{స్నేహితుడు} $\to$ \te{స్నేహితుడి}. \textbf{\te{స్నేహితుడి} \te{పేరు}} — \textquotedblleft{}the friend's name\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the noun changes shape before it does a job}]
Watch the shape of the noun, not just the ending. \te{స్నేహితుడు} stands on its own; \te{స్నేహితుడి} is the form that owns something. The ending does not land on the dictionary form — the noun leans toward it first, and you have already seen the same lean in \te{నేను} becoming \te{నాకు}. Look for it in front of -\te{కు} and -\te{లో} as well.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Possession by somebody other than you or me.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{snēhituḍi}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{snēhituḍi}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{nā pēru}, then \emph{snēhituḍi pēru}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{dēśaṁ}, then \emph{mariyu}, then \emph{cūḍu}, then say \emph{snēhituḍi}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{స్నేహితుడి} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}the friend's\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mā]{\te{మా} (mā) — our (not including you)}

\label{lesson:TE-C79-our}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{snēhituḍi} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{మా}}
\textbf{\te{మా}} (\emph{mā}) — \textquotedblleft{}our\textquotedblright{}, and \textbf{\te{మన}} (\emph{mana}) — \textquotedblleft{}our\textquotedblright{} as well.

Telugu splits a word English does not. \textbf{\te{మా}} leaves the listener out: my family, not yours. \textbf{\te{మన}} takes the listener in: our country, yours and mine.

\textbf{\te{మా} \te{ఇల్లు}} is my household. \textbf{\te{మన} \te{దేశం}} is the country we share. Choosing wrong is the mistake an examiner hears first.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two kinds of \emph{our}, and the difference between them.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mana}
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{mā kuṭumbaṁ}, then \emph{mana dēśaṁ}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{Bhāratadēśaṁ}, then \emph{kānī}, then \emph{rā}, then say \emph{mā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{మా} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}our (not including you)\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[atanu]{\te{అతను} (atanu) — he (and \te{ఆమె}, she)}

\label{lesson:TE-C79-he}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{mā} and \emph{mana} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{అతను}}
\textbf{\te{అతను}} (\emph{atanu}) — \textquotedblleft{}he\textquotedblright{}, \textbf{\te{ఆమె}} (\emph{āme}) — \textquotedblleft{}she\textquotedblright{}, \textbf{\te{వాళ్ళు}} (\emph{vāḷḷu}) — \textquotedblleft{}they\textquotedblright{}.

Until now you could speak about yourself and to one other person. You could not speak \emph{about} anybody, which is half of what an exam asks you to do.

All three start on the \textbf{\te{అ}-} of \te{అది} and \te{అక్కడ}: the far one, the one not here. \te{అతను} is literally \textquotedblleft{}that man\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the third person is where Telugu marks gender}]
You were told Telugu marks no gender on \textbf{I} or \textbf{you}, and that is still true. The third person is the exception: \textbf{\te{అతను} \te{వెళ్తాడు}} \textquotedblleft{}he goes\textquotedblright{} ends in \textbf{-\te{ఆడు}}, \textbf{\te{ఆమె} \te{వెళ్తుంది}} \textquotedblleft{}she goes\textquotedblright{} ends in \textbf{-\te{ఉంది}}, and \textbf{\te{వాళ్ళు} \te{వెళ్తారు}} \textquotedblleft{}they go\textquotedblright{} takes the same \textbf{-\te{ఆరు}} you already use for \te{మీరు}. Three endings, and the verb tells you who without the pronoun.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Somebody to talk about.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{atanu}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{āme}
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{atanu}, \emph{āme}, \emph{vāḷḷu}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{muppai}, then \emph{lēdā}, then \emph{caduvu}, then say \emph{atanu}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{అతను} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}he (and \te{ఆమె}, she)\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nannu]{\te{నన్ను} (nannu) — me (as the object)}

\label{lesson:TE-C79-me}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{atanu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{నన్ను}}
\textbf{\te{నన్ను}} (\emph{nannu}) — \textquotedblleft{}me\textquotedblright{}, when I am the one something is done to.

\te{నేను} is the \emph{I} that does. \te{నన్ను} is the \emph{me} that is done to: \textbf{\te{అతను} \te{నన్ను} \te{అడిగాడు}} — \textquotedblleft{}he asked me\textquotedblright{}.

The ending is \textbf{-\te{ను}}, and its partner \textbf{-\te{ని}} does the same on other nouns: \te{స్నేహితుడిని} \te{అడిగాను}, \textquotedblleft{}I asked the friend\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: people get marked, things usually do not}]
\textbf{\te{స్నేహితుడిని} \te{చూశాను}} — \textquotedblleft{}I saw the friend\textquotedblright{}, with \textbf{-\te{ని}} on the person. \textbf{\te{పుస్తకం} \te{చూశాను}} — \textquotedblleft{}I saw the book\textquotedblright{}, with nothing on the thing. Telugu marks a human object and leaves an inanimate one bare, which is very close to what Spanish does with its personal \emph{a}. Mark people; leave objects alone.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A pronoun on the receiving end.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nannu}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{nannu}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{nēnu}, then \emph{nannu}, and say which one is asked
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{avunā}, then \emph{enduku}, then \emph{veḷḷu}, then say \emph{nannu}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{నన్ను} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}me (as the object)\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[gāru]{\te{గారు} (gāru) — the respectful suffix on a name}

\label{lesson:TE-C79-garu}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{nannu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{గారు}}
\textbf{\te{గారు}} (\emph{gāru}) — the respect you attach to a name.

It is not a word you say alone. It rides on the end of a name or a role: \textbf{\te{రాము} \te{గారు}}, \textbf{\te{గురువు} \te{గారు}}, \textbf{\te{అమ్మ} \te{గారు}}.

You have had \te{మీరు} from your first introduction for respect in the pronoun. \te{గారు} is respect in the \emph{address}, and leaving it off where it belongs is heard as rudeness, not neutrality.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A way to say somebody's name that does not sound blunt.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{gāru}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{gāru}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{guruvu gāru}, then \emph{ammagāru}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{telusā}, then \emph{endukaṇṭē}, then \emph{rōju}, then say \emph{gāru}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{గారు} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}the respectful suffix on a name\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
